name: I Love Bees
title: The Beekeeping Site That Made Payphones Ring
claims: I Love Bees was an alternate reality game and viral marketing campaign for Halo 2 (2004) | 1
Created by 42 Entertainment; commissioned by Microsoft | 1
Honey jars with letters leading to the site and a countdown were mailed to people who had played ARGs | 1
Halo 2 trailers flashed a link to ilovebees.com after the Xbox.com URL | 1
Site looked like a hacked honey and beekeeping site with random characters and sentence fragments | 1
Webmaster Dana's weblog said something had gone wrong and the site was hacked | 1
The honey trail and trailer trail were not publicly connected for several weeks | 1
250,000 people viewed the site at launch in July 2004; more than 500,000 returned at each update | 1
More than three million visitors over three months; another count says two to three million unique visitors | 1
About 9,000 people actively participated in real-world aspects | 1
Imagined payphone scenario (7.51am, three minute ring, "Jim", search of phone number, discussion board) | 2
Game presented 210 pairs of GPS coordinates and time codes; players found they were payphones and ring times | 1
Some calls were live, made by an operator; players could interact with characters | 1
Texas payphone live call: guitar story, "MAKE HIM RUN!", clank, sandals, ninety seconds, 200 yard sprint, Wish You Were Here, smiles on muted lines in west coast cities | 2
Passwords had to be repeated so non-players were not scared by gunfire sounds | 1
One player stayed by a phone as Hurricane Frances was minutes away to recite answers | 1
Plot: ship crash, damaged AI Operator/Melissa moves to San Francisco-area server hosting the bee site | 1
Dana accidentally erased part of Melissa's memory; Melissa took webcam pictures and promised revenge; Dana left for China early | 1
SPDR, Pious Flea, Spider erased instead of Flea, Flea revealed as Seeker built by the Covenant | 1
Heroes break into military installation, deactivate Forerunner device; transmission alerts Covenant; ends with Covenant invading Earth | 1
Audio drama installments rewarded completed tasks | 1
42 Entertainment founded by Jordan Weisman, former creative director of Microsoft's Xbox division | 1
Earlier ARG The Beast promoted A.I.; name came from estimate of 666 images; Microsoft funded it; marketing connection almost excused | 1, 2
Bungie could not help with story; originally not canon; 2006 interview by Bungie content manager confirmed canon; later official books referenced it | 1
Conceived as a radio drama; War of the Worlds similarity intentional per Microsoft marketing director; payphones used to excite players | 1
Weisman toaster quote and "a game that is life itself" | 1
Players got emails, cell phone calls, arranged meetings; finale at four cinemas with Halo 2 play and commemorative DVD | 1
Analyst and former magazine editor quotes on its marketing effect; mainstream press coverage | 1
Target demographic younger males; middle-aged players too; some had no Halo experience | 1
Students held giant bee poster at third presidential debate on CNN, a rallying point for players | 2
Innovation Award at 5th Game Developers Choice Awards; Webby Award in Game-Related category | 1

The Guardian said ARGs seemed destined for the e-dustbin before this; broadband and interest in codes helped; marketers' fears of cost of failure eased; other developers interested; Bungie used Iris for Halo 3 | 1
Author Charles Leadbeater called it collective "We-Think" and mass-movement-like | 1
Vaporwave pioneer said it influenced them | 1
Designer's principle: challenge perception without shaking the foundations; avoid terrorism and bombs storylines; had to convince players an AI with a bee fetish was growing insane | 2
Sources differ: calls to payphones "across the US" vs players "around the world"; visitor counts differ | 1, 2
